checks.what: Confirm the canonical AgentX scoreboard and record today's top results for Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 and GLM-5.3 as a baseline.
checks.why: Almost every number here is stated against this board, and the founding sweep's fetch of inferencex.semianalysis.com returned a page calling itself an unofficial deployment. Without a recorded baseline, later claims of a lead cannot be judged.
checks.resolution: The canonical board is inferencex.semianalysis.com, run from SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX; the unofficial-copy notice is hidden markup shown only on other hosts. Baseline on 22 Nov, best total tokens per GPU at 50 tok/s per user or faster: Kimi K3 24.4k and Kimi K3.1 Pro 36.7k on GB300, GLM-5.3 23.2k on B300.

checks.what: Have InferenceForge's three SGLang fixes been reproduced by anyone else, or opened as pull requests against upstream SGLang?
checks.why: They sit in a personal fork. Upstreaming would be the first independent check on an outsider's agent-found gain, and a data point on how fast the commons absorbs one. On 26 Nov a research pass found the three fixes still sitting as pull requests on the author's own fork, with nothing opened upstream and no reproduction. Two overlap upstream work that predates the post.

checks.what: Is the Evolving Infra code actually public and runnable at github.com/mit-han-lab/EvolvingInfra?
checks.why: The project page says both open source and coming soon. A runnable release lets someone other than the authors test the 4x latency claim against Dynamo.
checks.resolution: Yes. The repository is public, with deployment and benchmark instructions and a path to reproduce the paper. Nobody outside has reproduced its headline numbers yet, and one open issue questions a table against a figure.

checks.what: Read first-hand the two papers reported as counter-evidence on local agent-written kernels: arXiv 2607.24762 (reported to lose to eager PyTorch on a DGX Spark) and arXiv 2611.12079 (a local 7B model's kernels at roughly break-even).
checks.why: They were relayed with too little detail to enter as signals. If they hold, they are the most direct evidence that the agent loop does not transfer to owned hardware.
checks.resolution: Out of scope. On 19 Nov the reader clarified that local means fitted to what you have (different devices), not on-device hardware, so the on-device question is no longer tracked.

checks.what: Does any public AgentX run, by Together or anyone else, match the up-to-2.6x lead Together claims for its compiler?
checks.why: A private lead that never appears on the public board cannot be told apart from a favourable baseline. If the open engines close it, the commons is keeping up. On 26 Nov, 22 days on, a research pass found no public run matching it, and heard of a closed engine from another team said to have led one board since September. Neither was opened first-hand; see W27.

checks.what: Has InferenceBench run a matched-budget search beside its newest agent entries, and has the gap (12.08x agent against 14.30x search) closed?
checks.why: This is the cleanest independent gauge of whether agents are getting better at the experimenting, not just the knowing. On 26 Nov the board was at version 1.0.8. The top agent was unchanged at 12.08x against 14.30x for search, and five newer entries all scored below it.

checks.what: Megakernels: any head-to-head on one model and chip, or any of vLLM, SGLang or Together changing course.
checks.why: Two camps shipped opposite bets in the same month. The next major model release is the natural test of whether fused paths can be regenerated fast enough.
checks.resolution: Hit on 18 Nov. vLLM's AMD team compared fused and stock decode for the same model on the same node, with graph replay on both: 1.20 to 2.26x for one user, shrinking as concurrency rose. No comparison against graphs plus PDL yet, so T1 stays open under W21.

checks.what: Any published evidence of compounding: gain per cycle rising, or a model trained on optimisation traces beating its teacher on a production task.
checks.why: This is the named condition for raising the RSI claim. InferenceForge said it would put its own models in the loop; Kernel-Smith and Meta already train on search traces.

checks.what: Any agent-driven optimisation loop on user-owned hardware (workstation, on-prem cluster, laptop) with a like-for-like baseline.
checks.why: The single result that would move the local claim most. Its continued absence is itself information.
checks.resolution: Out of scope. On 19 Nov the reader clarified that local means fitted to what you have (different devices), not on-device hardware, so the on-device question is no longer tracked.

checks.what: A provider publishing per-customer against class-level tuning on the same endpoints.
checks.why: The only numbers so far are 20 to 45%. One clean result above about 1.5x would change who is expected to capture the value.

checks.what: One system publishing like-for-like results on two chip families for the same model and traffic, with different winning optimisations on each.
checks.why: C2 now covers the chip as well as the traffic, and most of the hardware evidence is each team's account of its own bring-up. A same-system, two-chip comparison on the public board would test it directly.

checks.what: Any provider publishing what its loop costs per deployment (GPU-hours, tokens) next to the gain it bought.
checks.why: One figure exists: about 200 GPU-hours and 1.7B tokens for a bespoke engine. Whether per-customer tuning is a business turns on this number falling.

checks.what: A second workload owner, not a provider, describing its own loop on its own traffic.
checks.why: Decagon is the only one so far. If customers can do this themselves on rented GPUs, the provider's role shifts toward supplying the rig.

checks.what: A provider with no announced loop (Fireworks, Modal, Groq, Cerebras, a hyperscaler) describing one, or giving a credible reason not to.
checks.why: Three providers have described a loop. Silence from the rest is either catching up in private or a judgement that it does not pay.
checks.resolution: Hit, late: Alibaba's Herschel paper of 30 Sep, missed by the founding sweep, describes agents implementing and testing engine and kernel fixes across over 120 model variants and ten chip types, with expert review and canary rollout. Fireworks, Modal, Groq and Cerebras are still silent.

checks.what: Read Modal's post first-hand: was its draft model trained on the customer's own traffic, or on synthetic and target-model traces?
checks.why: The 20% figure is the cleanest number behind the per-customer claim, and a second check found Modal's other drafter post used synthetic data.
checks.resolution: Opened first-hand: the drafter was fine-tuned on coding traces the target model produced, for a shared coding service, and the recipe was reused across models. Nothing says it saw one customer's traffic, so the 20% is class-level.

checks.what: Any router published against the best fixed model in its own pool, on tasks someone else chose.
checks.why: Vendors report a third to three-fifths off; an outside test found no shipped router beating a cheap default. This is the comparison that would settle it.
checks.resolution: OpenRouter's public board runs its routers beside single models from the same pool on five public benchmarks. On Deep SWE several single models beat its coding router on quality and cost, and it says no router beats the best single model everywhere. W22 carries the live-session question.

checks.what: A tuned open model followed against the next general release on the same task.
checks.why: Tunes look good on the day and may be overtaken within weeks. Whether tuning is a lever or a treadmill turns on this.
checks.resolution: Yes, and it was overtaken. Harvey's August tune of one open model scored 19.7% on its legal benchmark; by November an untuned general model scored 27.1%. Harvey answered by tuning four newer open models, the best reaching 30.3%.

checks.what: Open two leads a sub-agent saw but could not date: Cerebras on its autoresearch loop cheating, and an LMSYS post on an internal system called Infer-forge. Add them to the roster if they describe a loop.
checks.why: The reader asked that no team building the loop be missed. A provider and an open-engine team may both be absent.
checks.resolution: Both describe loops and are now on the roster: Infer-forge, an internal agent harness around SGLang (28 Aug), and Cerebras's autoresearch runs on fitting a large model onto consumer GPUs (19 Mar).

checks.what: Any provider publishing how long and how much it takes to get a new model from release to tuned serving, with or without agents.
checks.why: With many models this is the cost that repeats. Day-zero support is claimed by several teams; none has given a time or a price. On 22 Nov the public board showed the open engines take about two weeks to tune a new model; a provider's own time and cost are still unpublished. On 26 Nov the closest figures were one company's 401 minutes from public weights to a live endpoint, untuned, and an individual's 41-hour agent campaign costing about $400 of GPU time. Still nothing from a provider on tuned serving.

checks.what: A mixture-of-experts model measured in a real engine with and without speculation from 1 to 128 concurrent, or the Doubleword simulator compared with a real engine.
checks.why: Measured tables show speculation fading with load. A cost model says that on mixture-of-experts models it starts near zero and grows, and its author says most new models are of that kind. Which is right decides how a provider sets lever 4 for each model, and whether a simulator can stand in for part of the rig. On 20 Nov an outside run of Kimi K3 in two engines covered 1 to 64 concurrent and showed the usual fade. Still wanted: beyond 64, a draft length that follows the load, and longer prompts. On 26 Nov a different simulator, BLIS, was found to predict real runs within 6.7% for scheduling policies. The Doubleword one is still unchecked. A research pass on 26 Nov also reported three measured mixture-of-experts sets in which speculation held up as batches filled: a vLLM post on adaptive verification of 14 August, a Red Hat post of 16 April, and the body of arXiv 2610.40287. None was opened first-hand; if they hold, T10's lean is wrong.

checks.what: On one NVIDIA chip, a model's fused decode path measured against CUDA Graphs plus PDL on the same traces, from 1 to 16 concurrent.
checks.why: Together says graphs plus PDL recover 98% of a megakernel's gain; on AMD chips, graph replay alone left 1.2 to 2.3x for one user. A provider serving many models needs to know whether per-model fused code pays.

checks.what: A router compared with the best single model in its pool on live agent sessions rather than benchmark tasks, with the pricing of cached tokens stated.
checks.why: On public tasks a vendor's own router lost to the best single models. Live sessions vary more, which is the case routing is meant to win. Whether a provider should build a router or simply pick its default well turns on this. On 26 Nov: an outside index compared six routers with the best model in each pool on benchmark tasks and all lost, but sessions were not live and cached tokens were not priced. One vendor reports a live test with its router just ahead of a model in its own pool.

checks.what: vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp or MLX supporting a looped model upstream with depth chosen per token or per request, rather than a fixed number of passes.
checks.why: vLLM runs Ouro at its full four passes and ignores the learned early exit, Inkling 2 Mini supports only three passes, and the rest lives in research forks. Upstream support is what would make depth a lever a provider can pull.

checks.what: A looped and a dense model of equal quality served side by side in one engine, with memory and throughput per GPU at several batch sizes and context lengths.
checks.why: It would settle T11 and test C11 where a provider lives: whether a looped model's saving on weights survives its cache at real batch sizes and prompt lengths.

checks.what: Cross-model cache transfer merged into vLLM, SGLang or llm-d, shipped by a provider or a router, or tested by an outside group on multi-turn agent sessions with tool calls.
checks.why: Three research systems move a cache between open models faster than a re-read. If one reaches an engine, a router can change model mid-session inside an open pool, which loosens the tie that lever 1 and C9 rest on. Until then it is a lab result on small models. On 26 Nov the first translator's code and weights were public as a separate package that injects a translated cache into stock vLLM. A newer paper extends translation to compressed and linear attention and warns that re-translating across turns collapses. Still no merge and no outside test.

checks.what: Read RSIBench-Infra in full: which agents and baselines, how many of its 20 tasks are LLM serving, and whether results above 1.10x beat tuned engines or only official recipes.
checks.why: Its abstract says two-thirds of task results passed a validated 1.10x end to end, measured independently at up to 32 accelerators. That is the kind of evidence C1 says would raise it, but the abstract does not say against what.

checks.what: Open TileRT's own pages and the public board: has a closed binary led single-user agent serving since September, and has any open engine matched it?
checks.why: A lead held for two months by a closed engine would be the clearest case against the commons keeping up. It was reported by a research pass and its pages have timed out twice.
